commons.title: William S. Soule - Pacers son.jpg
commons.description:
Pacer's son
Pacer's (Iron Sack), head chief of the Kiowa-Apaches, son.

The name of this young man is not given, but Soule took him in two poses which are almost identical.[...] Notice the hair-pipe breastplate, brass hatchet, silver beads, silver clain tied to his scalp lock, and beaver or otter fur wrapped around one braid.— Smithsonian Institution, Bureau of American Ethnology, In: Wilbur Sturtevant Nye, Plains Indian raiders : the final phases of warfare from the Arkansas to the Red River, with original photographs by William S. Soule. University of Oklahoma Press, 1st edition, 1968, ISBN 0806111755, p378.
commons.editorial_reason: Description identifies him as the son of the Kiowa-Apache chief and visibly shows hair-pipe, bead, metal, and fur adornment.

commons.title: William S. Soule - Issue day at Camp Supply.jpg
commons.description:
Issue day at Camp Supply
This is probably the first issue of rations and annuities at Camp Supply. For years this photograph was believed to have been made at Fort Sill, but more recent information places Camp Supply as the site. This identification comes from Morgan Otis, a construction engineer and a descendant of the Fort Marion Kiowa prisoner, Zotom (Zontam), and of Pacer, the Kiowa-Apache chief.[...] The agency ration issues initially were flour, sugar, coffee, dried fruit, and desiccated vegetables. Beef was issued later after the buffalo had become scarce.— Wilbur S. Nye collection, In: Wilbur Sturtevant Nye, Plains Indian raiders : the final phases of warfare from the Arkansas to the Red River, with original photographs by William S. Soule. University of Oklahoma Press, 1st edition, 1968, ISBN 0806111755, p352.
commons.editorial_reason: Shows a generic ration distribution; the caption does not specifically identify the people pictured as Plains Apache.

commons.title: William S. Soule - Black Hawk.jpg
commons.description:
Black Hawk
It is unfortunate that nothing is known today concerning this Kiowa-Apache, for he is a fine-looking man and his face shows much character. He had a reputation of being friendly and co-operative.He is waring some expensive ornamentation and a Washington medal, and has the shoulder insignia of a major or lieutnant colonel.— Smithsonian Institution, Bureau of American Ethnology, In: Wilbur Sturtevant Nye, Plains Indian raiders : the final phases of warfare from the Arkansas to the Red River, with original photographs by William S. Soule. University of Oklahoma Press, 1st edition, 1968, ISBN 0806111755, p382.
commons.editorial_reason: Description identifies Black Hawk as Kiowa-Apache, and he visibly wears elaborate traditional ornamentation and a medal.

commons.title: William S. Soule - Pacers nephew.jpg
commons.description:
Pacer's nephew
Pacer's (Iron Sack), head chief of the Kiowa-Apaches, nephew.

[...]Note the neckpiece made of short pieces of hair pipe. John C. Ewers
states that this type of ornament, actually made of conch shell, was a rarity.— Smithsonian Institution, Bureau of American Ethnology, In: Wilbur Sturtevant Nye, Plains Indian raiders : the final phases of warfare from the Arkansas to the Red River, with original photographs by William S. Soule. University of Oklahoma Press, 1st edition, 1968, ISBN 0806111755, p380.
commons.editorial_reason: Description identifies him as the Kiowa-Apache chief's nephew, and the visible hair-pipe neckpiece is attributed cultural adornment.
